match.reason: The closest bank point, on developing an argument across essay paragraphs, covers building a thesis in an analytical essay rather than the order of a persuasive text such as anecdote, evidence, then call to action, so it is related but not the same idea.

draft.title: How arguments are structured
card: Writers order the parts of an argument on purpose. Each part is placed to build the reader's response step by step.
Anecdote first
a short story or personal case at the start. It makes the issue feel real and gets the reader to care before any facts appear.
Evidence next
facts, statistics or expert views that follow. They give the reader reasons to accept the contention once they are interested.
Call to action last
a closing appeal that tells the reader what to do or think. It turns the feeling and reasons built earlier into a response.
draft.remember: Ask why each part sits where it does, and how it builds on the part before.

a.q: A writer opens an article on bus cuts with a story about Ayesha, who now walks two hours to work. What is the main reason for starting this way?
opts: To make the issue personal before the facts arrive
To prove the cuts have harmed most commuters
To tell readers exactly what action to take
To show that the writer has expert knowledge
a.why: An anecdote at the start makes the reader care about the issue, which prepares them for the evidence that follows. One person's story cannot prove that most commuters are harmed, so that option is the tempting wrong answer.
a.clue: Think about what the reader feels before any facts are given.

b.q: Mia's opinion piece on school start times ends with the line: 'Write to your local MP this week and demand later starts.' What does this closing part do within the structure of her argument?
opts: It turns the reader's agreement into a response
It gives the main statistics that support her case
It introduces a personal story to engage the reader
It states the opposing view so she can reject it
b.why: A call to action comes after the story and evidence, and it asks the reader to act on what they now believe. It gives no new evidence and no personal story. Those usually come earlier in the argument.
b.clue: The line tells the reader to do something, and it comes last.

a.best: To make the issue personal before the facts arrive

b.best: It turns the reader's agreement into a response

problems.detail: The card presents 'Anecdote first', 'Evidence next' and 'Call to action last' as the way arguments are ordered, not as one common example. The chapter frames this order as 'such as'. Students may assume every argument follows this sequence and force it onto pieces structured differently, for example ones that open with a rebuttal or a statistic. The card should say this is a common pattern and that structures vary.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match the card. The card presents anecdote, then evidence, then call to action as a fixed order rather than one common pattern, which could mislead students analysing differently structured pieces.

proposal.title: How arguments are structured
card: Writers order the parts of an argument on purpose, so each part builds on the last. One common pattern is anecdote, then evidence, then a call to action, but structures vary. Some pieces open with a statistic or a rebuttal instead.
Anecdote
a short story or personal case. Placed at the start, it makes the issue feel real and gets the reader to care before any facts appear.
Evidence
facts, statistics or expert views. Placed after an anecdote, they give an interested reader reasons to accept the contention.
Call to action
a closing appeal that tells the reader what to do or think. It turns the feeling and reasons built earlier into a response.
proposal.remember: Ask why each part sits where it does, and how it builds on the part before.
